context: The excerpt describes Sirius as a human-in-the-loop framework for deploying partially autonomous robots. The robot handles decisions in situations where its policy is reliable, while a human operator monitors execution and takes over during difficult or potentially failing situations. This division of labor is intended to provide safe, consistently successful task execution while allowing the robot to improve over time and reduce human workload. Sirius learns from deployment data by estimating human trust from intervention behavior and assigning different weights to training samples. context: RaC (Recovery and Correction) is an iterative imitation-learning data-collection strategy that combines human-provided recovery segments with corrective segments and full expert demonstrations. context: The excerpt describes Genie Centurion (GCENT) as a real-robot training and supervision framework designed to improve data yield relative to human effort. Its Task Sentinel is a multimodal model that monitors image observations and task instructions, detects whether an atomic step has been completed, and automatically advances when successful. If a step remains incomplete beyond a predefined timeout, it places the robot in “Awaiting Intervention” and requests human help. In Human-Gated mode, the operator intervenes when errors occur; as policy performance improves, Sentinel allows one operator to supervise multiple robots and request assistance only when necessary. When intervention is needed, the operator can rewind up to three seconds using the robot’s state buffer, apply physical corrections, and provide a targeted demonstration. The policy is trained only on these human intervention segments, concentrating supervision on corrective, high-value data rather than complete passive trajectories. Its one-human-to-many-robots supervision model relies on the Task Sentinel, a vision-language module that monitors autonomous robot execution, predicts whether a task has been completed, and requests human intervention when needed. Rather than controlling robots continuously, the human acts mainly as a guardian who intervenes when a policy fails or is likely to fail. GCENT then uses a rewind mechanism to return the robot to a recent valid state, enabling corrective demonstrations and greater coverage of failure and recovery states. The paper reports real-world experiments in which GCENT achieves up to 40% higher task success rates than existing data-collection methods and reaches comparable performance with less than half the data. As deployment progresses, the framework is intended to increase single-robot success rates while reducing intervention rates, allowing one operator to supervise more robots. The excerpt also states that the authors quantify the data yield-to-effort ratio in multi-robot settings, supporting GCENT’s potential for scalable and cost-efficient robot policy training.
